entry.title: Engineering Applications of Fiber-Reinforced TPMS Lattices: From Theory to Practice

link.title: Engineering Applications of Fiber-Reinforced TPMS Lattices: From Theory to Practice

entry.content:
The promise of TPMS (triply periodic minimal surface) lattices has always been their exceptional structural efficiency for lightweight energy absorption. But a critical question remained: How do chopped fiber reinforcement and thermal post-processing actually affect their mechanical response in real applications?

Our latest findings provide quantitative answers.

We systematically tested gyroid TPMS lattices across five polymeric materials—VeroWhite, Nylon 12, ABS, PLA-CF, and PPA-CF—at relative densities from 20-40%. The results are significant for design engineers:

Performance Metrics That Matter:

Annealed PPA-CF gyroids achieve specific energy absorption of 24-25 kJ/kg at densities of 200-430 kg/m³. To put this in context: this is comparable to metallic TPMS structures, but at substantially lower weight. For aerospace and automotive applications, that weight savings translates directly to efficiency gains.

The Processing-Performance Link:

Thermal annealing of chopped carbon fiber-reinforced lattices isn’t just a minor improvement—it’s transformative:

  • Peak stress increases by ~40%

  • Toughness improves by up to 60%

  • Post-yield deformation behavior fundamentally changes

But there’s a trade-off engineers must account for: our finite element analysis reveals elevated stress localization and increased plastic strains in fiber-reinforced lattices. This explains the experimentally observed post-elastic ductility trade-offs.

Application Prospects:

The figure above illustrates where these structures matter most:

  1. Aerospace: Structural damping and lightweight panels

  2. Automotive: Crash energy absorption systems and vibration isolation components

  3. Marine: Wave manipulation structures for drag reduction on ships and submarines

  4. Space: High energy absorption legs for soft landing of spacecrafts

  5. Civil/Mechanical: Vibration isolation and acoustic damping systems

The Design Takeaway:

Chopped fiber reinforcement combined with thermal post-processing doesn’t just incrementally improve TPMS lattice performance—it fundamentally modifies deformation behavior. This enables high-performance, lightweight architectures, but requires coordinated control of:

  • Relative density (we studied 20-40%)

  • Fiber reinforcement type and content

  • Thermal post-processing parameters

For engineers working on lightweight structural systems, the message is clear: fiber-reinforced, annealed TPMS lattices offer a viable path to metallic-level performance at polymer weight—but you must design for the altered stress distributions and post-yield behavior.

Full technical paper with experimental methodology, FEA validation, and detailed process-structure-property relationships:

https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01791-9

Hussain, S., Mehraj, H., Moustafa, M. et al. “Do chopped fibers matter? Process–structure–property relationships and thermal annealing effects in fiber-reinforced TPMS lattices.” Progress in Additive Manufacturing 11, 8199–8219 (2026).

entry.title: Do Chopped Carbon Fibers Actually Improve 3D-Printed Lattices? (We Tested It)

link.title: Do Chopped Carbon Fibers Actually Improve 3D-Printed Lattices? (We Tested It)

entry.content:
If you’ve spent any time reading about 3D printing and architected materials recently, you’ve probably seen the hype around Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) structures.

Because of their zero-mean-curvature geometry, structures like the Gyroid don’t have the sharp nodes or corners found in standard strut lattices. This lets them distribute stress evenly and absorb huge amounts of energy without collapsing prematurely.

Naturally, the next step engineers take to push performance further is to throw chopped carbon fibers into the filament. Higher stiffness, higher strength — problem solved, right?

Not quite.

In practice, the literature on chopped fiber TPMS lattices has been surprisingly mixed. In some tests, short carbon fibers make parts stiffer; in others, the added brittleness actually makes the printed lattice perform worse than its unreinforced polymer counterpart under heavy compression.

To figure out what’s actually going on, our team at NYU Abu Dhabi put together a systematic study looking at the intersection of material, density, and post-processing.

Here is what we found.

The Experiment: 5 Materials, 3 Densities, and Heat Treatment

We 3D-printed Gyroid lattices across relative densities ranging from 20% to 40% using five distinct material systems:

  • VeroWhite (PolyJet)
  • Nylon 12 (Selective Laser Sintering)
  • ABS (Fused Filament Fabrication / FFF)
  • PLA-CF (10% carbon fiber by volume)
  • PPA-CF (Polyphthalamide with 15% carbon fiber by volume)

We also took a subset of the PPA-CF lattices and subjected them to a post-print thermal annealing process (80°C for 8–12 hours) to see if heat-treating could unlock latent mechanical performance.

Key Takeaway 1: Reinforcement Needs Density

At low relative densities (20%), material choice barely made a difference. The architecture itself dominates the behavior, meaning thin walls flex and deform regardless of what they’re made of.

However, as relative density increased to 30% and 40%, the performance of the carbon fiber-reinforced PPA (PPA-CF) pulled ahead drastically. At 40% density, as-built PPA-CF gyroids achieved a peak stress outperforming PLA-CF by nearly 50%, sustaining load through a smooth, progressive strain-hardening regime.

Key Takeaway 2: Thermal Annealing is the Real Game-Changer

While adding chopped carbon fibers helps, post-print heat treatment is what truly elevates performance.

When we thermally annealed the PPA-CF gyroids, we saw:

  • Peak stress increase by ~40%
  • Toughness (energy absorption) jump by up to 60%
  • Specific Energy Absorption (SEA) values hitting 24–25 kJ/kg

To put that 24–25 kJ/kg number into perspective, it places these lightweight polymer-composite lattices into the performance envelope typically reserved for metallic TPMS structures (like titanium or steel lattices) — but at a fraction of the weight.

Key Takeaway 3: The Ductility Trade-Off

There is no free lunch in materials science.

While annealing significantly boosts peak load capacity and stiffness, it alters how the lattice fails. FEA simulations showed that fiber reinforcement increases localized stress concentration and plastic strain along load-bearing curves.

As a result, annealed PPA-CF lattices trade off some post-yield ductility. Instead of a perfectly flat, predictable crushing plateau, they experience minor stress drops corresponding to localized internal shear planes.

If your goal is absolute maximum strength and lightweight energy dissipation (think aerospace crash protection or defense applications), annealed PPA-CF is an exceptional choice. If you need a completely smooth, constant crushing force, unreinforced or untreated polymers might still have a role to play.

Final Thoughts

Architected metamaterials aren’t just about tweaking CAD geometry. The interplay between inner topology, fiber orientation, and thermal post-processing dictates how these parts actually behave in the real world.

By coordinating relative density with post-print annealing, chopped-fiber polymer lattices can bridge the gap between heavy metals and compliant plastics.

For the full deep dive, FEA models, and raw dataset, check out our paper published in Progress in Additive Manufacturing:

🔗 https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01791-9

Datasets: https://zenodo.org/records/18457274 and

Reference

Hussain, S., Mehraj, H., Moustafa, M. et al. Do chopped fibers matter? Process–structure–property relationships and thermal annealing effects in fiber-reinforced TPMS lattices.Prog Addit Manuf (2026). https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01791-9

entry.title: Do Chopped Fibers Matter?
entry.content:
When we think about lightweight structural materials, we often imagine a trade‑off: polymers are light but mechanically limited, while metals are strong but heavy. Architected metamaterials — especially TPMS lattices — have been challenging that assumption for years. But one question has remained surprisingly unanswered:

What happens when we combine TPMS architecture with chopped‑fiber reinforcement and thermal annealing?

Our newly published paper, “Do chopped fibers matter? Process‑structure‑property relationships and thermal annealing effects in fiber‑reinforced TPMS lattices,” takes this question head‑on. And the results turned out to be far more dramatic — and far more promising — than expected.

Why TPMS lattices are special

TPMS (triply periodic minimal surface) lattices, like the gyroid, are not your typical strut‑based structures. Their continuous curvature, smooth load paths, and absence of sharp nodes give them:

  • predictable, progressive deformation

  • high energy absorption

  • reduced stress concentrations

  • excellent stability under compression

They’re already used in damping, impact protection, aerospace components, and bio‑inspired designs. But almost all prior studies focused on unreinforced polymers — PLA, ABS, Nylon — leaving a major gap in understanding how short‑fiber composites behave inside these architectures.

What we set out to investigate

We asked four fundamental questions:

  1. Do chopped carbon fibers change how TPMS lattices deform and fail?

  2. How does reinforcement affect stiffness, strength, toughness, and energy absorption across densities?

  3. Can thermal annealing unlock hidden performance in fiber‑reinforced TPMS?

  4. Do numerical simulations reflect the same stress localization and plastic strain patterns we see experimentally?

To answer these, we built and tested gyroid lattices using five materials:

  • VeroWhite

  • Nylon 12

  • ABS

  • PLA‑CF (10% chopped carbon fiber)

  • PPA‑CF (15% chopped carbon fiber)

Each printed at 20%, 30%, and 40% relative density, followed by quasi‑static compression testing and finite element analysis.

What we discovered

1. Chopped fibers fundamentally alter deformation behavior

Fiber‑reinforced lattices didn’t just get stronger — they behaved differently.

“Finite element analysis reveals elevated stress localization and increased plastic strains in fiber‑reinforced lattices…”

This means the architecture and reinforcement interact in complex ways. The gyroid’s membrane‑bending mix creates stress states that chopped fibers amplify, redirect, or stabilize depending on density and processing.

2. Annealing transforms PPA‑CF into a high‑performance metamaterial

Annealing PPA‑CF at 80 °C for 8–12 hours produced striking improvements:

  • ~40% increase in peak stress

  • Up to 60% increase in toughness

  • Higher stiffness and yield strength

  • Modified post‑yield stability (stronger but less ductile)

“Post-print thermal annealing of PPA-CF increases its peak stress by ~40% and toughness by up to 60%…”

This is one of the clearest demonstrations that processing matters as much as architecture and material.

3. Energy absorption approaches metallic TPMS — at polymer weight

Annealed PPA‑CF gyroids reached:

  • 24–25 kJ/kg specific energy absorption (SEA)

  • Densities of only 200–430 kg/m³

These values are comparable to aluminum and titanium TPMS structures — but at a fraction of the mass.

This positions fiber‑reinforced TPMS composites as lightweight alternatives to metallic metamaterials for crash protection, damping, and structural energy absorption.

4. Relative density amplifies composite advantages

At low density (20%), architecture dominates.
At high density (40%), reinforcement + densification produce nonlinear jumps in peak stress and toughness.

This suggests a design rule:
If you want maximum benefit from chopped fibers, go above 30% relative density.

5. A clear material hierarchy emerges

Across all metrics:

Annealed PPA‑CF > As‑built PPA‑CF > PLA‑CF > ABS ≈ Nylon12 > VeroWhite

The gap widens as density increases.

Why this matters for the future of architected materials

This study shows that TPMS mechanics cannot be predicted from base material tensile properties alone. The gyroid’s continuous curvature creates complex stress states that interact strongly with:

  • fiber orientation

  • interlayer bonding

  • crystallinity

  • annealing‑induced microstructural changes

The takeaway is simple but powerful:

Performance emerges from architecture × material × processing — not any single factor.

This opens the door to designing polymer‑based metamaterials that rival metals in energy absorption, stiffness‑to‑weight ratio, and structural stability.

Where this research can be applied

The results point toward promising uses in:

  • crash energy absorption

  • vibration isolation

  • aerospace and automotive damping

  • lightweight structural panels

  • sound insulation

  • protective enclosures

  • robotics and soft‑mechanics interfaces

Anywhere weight matters — and performance matters more.

Read the paper & explore the dataset

📄 Full paper:
Progress in Additive Manufacturing
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01791-9

📂 Open dataset:
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18457274

entry.title: When Chopped Fibers Meet Gyroid Lattices: Unlocking Metallic-Level Energy Absorption in 3D Printed Polymers

link.title: When Chopped Fibers Meet Gyroid Lattices: Unlocking Metallic-Level Energy Absorption in 3D Printed Polymers

entry.content:
Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) lattices—particularly the gyroid architecture—have emerged as a transformative class of architected metamaterials. By decoupling structural performance from the intrinsic properties of the base material, they offer exceptional stiffness-to-weight ratios and progressive energy absorption.

But as we push the boundaries of additive manufacturing (AM), a critical question remains: How do we push polymeric TPMS lattices to perform closer to metallic structures without sacrificing their lightweight advantages?

In our recently published paper in Progress in Additive Manufacturing, my colleagues and I at NYU Abu Dhabi systematically investigated the process–structure–property relationships of fiber-reinforced TPMS lattices (Figure 1). Specifically, we looked at whether adding chopped carbon fibers, combined with post-print thermal annealing, could fundamentally alter the deformation mechanics of gyroid structures.

Here is a technical summary of what we found.

The Experimental Matrix

We didn't just look at one material. To isolate the effects of fiber reinforcement and architecture, we fabricated gyroid TPMS lattices across three relative densities (20%, 30%, and 40%) using five distinct polymeric systems:

  • VeroWhite (PolyJet)

  • Nylon 12 (SLS)

  • ABS (FFF)

  • PLA-CF (10% chopped carbon fiber, FFF)

  • PPA-CF (15% chopped carbon fiber, FFF)

We subjected these to quasi-static compression testing and validated the deformation mechanisms using non-linear Finite Element Analysis (FEA). We also applied a post-print thermal annealing process (80 °C for 8 hours) specifically to the PPA-CF specimens to unlock latent mechanical performance.

Key Discoveries: The Synergy of Density and Fibers

Our results showed that simply adding fibers to a low-density lattice isn't enough. The true magic happens at the intersection of high relative density and fiber reinforcement.

The 40% Density Threshold: At lower densities (20%), architectural compliance dominates, and material differences are less pronounced. However, at 40% relative density, the PPA-CF (CF15) lattices exhibited massive strain-hardening. The compressive stress increased from ~5 MPa at yield to over 15 MPa at a strain of 0.5, vastly outperforming neat polymers like ABS and Nylon 12, which suffered from premature collapse or stress plateaus.

Progressive Collapse: Unlike more brittle composites (like PLA-CF) or compliant resins (VeroWhite), the as-built PPA-CF gyroids exhibited extended plateau regions. The chopped fibers promoted effective stress redistribution, leading to a progressive, layer-by-layer collapse ideal for energy absorption.

The Game Changer: Thermal Annealing

The most significant breakthrough of our study was the effect of thermal post-processing on the PPA-CF lattices. Annealing at 80 °C fundamentally modified the post-yield behavior:

  • Peak Stress: Increased by ~40%.

  • Toughness (Energy Absorption): Increased by up to 60%.

Why does this happen? Annealing increases crystallinity in the PPA matrix, relaxes residual stresses from the FFF process, and drastically improves the fiber–matrix interfacial bonding.

Approaching Metallic Performance

To put these numbers into perspective, we calculated the Specific Energy Absorption (SEA).

Annealed PPA-CF gyroids achieved an SEA of 24–25 kJ/kg at densities of just 200–430 kg/m³.

To contextualize this: these values are highly competitive with single-phase aluminum and titanium alloy TPMS structures, and they achieve similar energy absorption to steel-based metamaterials at a density reduction of nearly 1,500 kg/m³ (Figure 2). We effectively bridged the performance gap between lightweight polymeric foams and heavy metallic lattices.

The Engineering Trade-Off: Strength vs. Ductility

As materials engineers know, there is no free lunch. While thermal annealing unlocked massive gains in peak strength and toughness, it introduced a critical trade-off.

Our FEA and experimental data showed that annealing reduces the post-elastic ductility of the base composite. Instead of a smooth, continuous plateau, the annealed lattices (particularly at 30% density) exhibited localized stress drops and inner shear plane failures. The fibers, while highly aligned in the extrusion direction to resist in-plane membrane stresses, are poorly oriented to resist out-of-plane shear stresses once significant plasticization occurs.

The takeaway for design: If your application requires a perfectly smooth, constant plateau stress, as-built PPA-CF or ductile neat polymers might be preferable. But if your design criteria prioritize maximum peak load-bearing capacity and total energy absorption per unit weight, annealed PPA-CF is the superior choice.

Conclusion

Our study demonstrates that material selection is just as critical as geometric design in architected metamaterials. By coordinating the control of relative density, chopped carbon fiber reinforcement, and thermal post-processing, we can engineer polymer-based TPMS lattices that rival metallic structures in energy absorption, while maintaining a fraction of the weight.

This opens up exciting new avenues for lightweight impact protection, aerospace structural components, and biomedical implants.

📖 Read the full open-access paper here: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01791-9

Data and supplementary materials are available on Zenodo.

What are your thoughts on the trade-offs of thermal annealing in FFF composites? Have you experimented with post-processing TPMS structures for specific energy absorption? Let me know in the comments or connect with me on Website/Bluesky/Lens.

#AdditiveManufacturing, #Metamaterials, #3DPrinting, #MaterialsScience, #TPMS, #Engineering
entry.summary: By combining chopped carbon fiber reinforcement with thermal post-processing, 3D-printed polymer gyroids can achieve metallic-level energy absorption at a fraction of the weight of aluminum or titanium.

entry.title: What Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) of NiTi TPMS Lattices Taught Me: Failures, Fixes, and Lessons From the Melt Pool

link.title: What Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) of NiTi TPMS Lattices Taught Me: Failures, Fixes, and Lessons From the Melt Pool

entry.content:
NiTi is one of those materials that looks magical in theory — shape memory, superelasticity, biocompatibility — and deceptively difficult in practice. Combine it with TPMS lattices, which have huge surface‑area‑to‑volume ratios and complex curvature, and you get a structure that could revolutionize implants, energy absorbers, and adaptive systems… if you can actually print it.

Over the past few years, I spent a lot of time trying to print NiTi TPMS lattices that simply refused to behave. Some warped off the build plate. Others balled up mid‑print. A few looked acceptable on the outside and turned out to be microstructurally chaotic under SEM.

I designed the CAD models, selected the process parameters, and analyzed the microstructures, while a dedicated research engineer operated the EOS M400‑4. These failures — and the process of understanding them — became the foundation of the papers I later published.

This article is the story behind those papers: the problems, the fixes, and what they taught me about NiTi, melt‑pool physics, and the hidden influence of geometry.

1. Delamination: When the Print Peels Itself Off the Plate

One of the earliest and most frustrating failures was delamination (Figure 1). After roughly 90-100 layers, the TPMS structures would detach from the Ti‑alloy build plate. The recoater blade would catch the warped surface, and the print had to be stopped.

Figure 1: Schematic representation of a thin NiTi layer delaminating and peeling away from the build plate substrate due to thermal mismatch and accumulated residual stresses.

The root cause turned out to be simple: NiTi and Ti‑alloy expand and contract differently. The thermal mismatch created residual stresses strong enough to lift the part off the plate.

The fix was surprisingly straightforward: 👉 Use a NiTi build plate instead of Ti‑alloy.

Once we switched, delamination disappeared.

🔹 Lesson: Build‑plate metallurgy matters as much as laser parameters.

2. Balling and Improper Fusion: The Melt Pool Fighting Back

Balling was everywhere — tiny spheres, broken tracks, uneven surfaces (Figure 2). Under SEM, the surfaces looked like miniature meteor fields. Some spheres were 20–40 µm, others exceeded 80 µm depending on density and scan strategy.

Figure 1. Scanning electron micrograph of the surface morphology of LPBF‑fabricated NiTi TPMS lattice showing characteristic imperfections. Spherical balls and uneven surfaces indicate incomplete melting and spattering, while pores and laser melt tracks reveal localized lack‑of‑fusion regions. These features collectively illustrate melt‑pool instability and non‑uniform solidification typical of NiTi under sub‑optimal process parameters. [Ref. 3]

The causes were classic LPBF issues:

  • Insufficient energy density

  • High scan speeds

  • Poor wetting of molten NiTi on the previous layer

  • Rapid heat loss due to complex TPMS curvature

By systematically adjusting laser power, scan speed, and energy density, we eventually stabilized the melt pool. Higher power and slower scanning reduced balling dramatically.

But the real insight was this: 👉 Balling is a melt‑pool stability problem, not just a parameter problem.

🔹 Lesson: If the melt pool is unstable, no parameter chart will save you.

3. Geometry Is a Hidden Process Parameter

Gyroid and primitive lattices behaved very differently, even under identical parameters. Gyroids consistently produced rougher surfaces, more balling, and more uneven melt tracks.

The reason became clear when we compared their surface areas (for the same unit cell size):

  • Primitive (61.1 mm²)

  • Gyroid (121.3 mm²)

The gyroid’s massive surface area drastically increased heat dissipation, which accelerated solidification and destabilized the melt pool.

👉 Geometry shapes the thermal field — and the thermal field shapes the microstructure.

🔹 Lesson: In LPBF of NiTi, geometry is a process parameter.

4. Microstructural Inhomogeneity: A Map of the Thermal History

When we sectioned the samples and examined them under SEM, the microstructures were anything but uniform. We observed:

  • Equiaxed grains

  • Dendritic regions

  • Columnar grains

  • Abrupt transitions within microns

This wasn’t stochastic noise — it was a direct imprint of the local cooling rate and thermal gradient. Primitive lattices showed more mixed grain structures, whereas gyroids tended toward columnar growth due to directional heat flux (Refer Ref. 2).

👉 Microstructure is the most honest record of what the melt pool experienced.

🔹 Lesson: If you want to understand your process, study the grain transitions.

5. Scan Strategy and Density: The Subtle Influencers

In our Materials paper, we explored how scan strategy and relative density affected imperfections. Two surprising findings stood out:

  1. Inclined (45°) scan strategies produced the most severe balling.

  2. Higher relative densities unexpectedly produced larger balling diameters.

These results showed that:

  • Scan vector orientation fundamentally alters heat‑flow direction

  • Density changes the localized thermal mass

👉 Energy density alone cannot predict print quality.

🔹 Lesson: Scan strategy and density quietly shape melt‑pool behavior behind the scenes.

What These Failures Taught Me

Looking back, the most valuable insights didn’t come from the successful prints — they came from the failures.

  1. NiTi demands metallurgical compatibility. Even the build plate matters.

  2. TPMS geometry is a process parameter. Surface area and curvature dictate the life or death of your melt pool.

  3. Defects are clues. Balling, porosity, and grain transitions reveal the true thermal history of your part.

  4. Collaboration accelerates learning. Conversations with researchers saved us months of blind trial‑and‑error.

In LPBF of NiTi, successful prints teach you what worked once. Failed prints teach you how the material actually behaves.

💬 Let’s Connect

Have you run into similar challenges printing NiTi or complex TPMS structures? What melt‑pool or delamination issues have you battled in your own work?

Share your experiences — I’d love to compare notes.

🌐 Website: www.shahadathussain.com
✉️ Email: contact@shahadathussain.com

References

  1. Hussain, S., Alagha, A.N., Haidemenopoulos, G.N., & Zaki, W. (2023). Microstructural and surface analysis of NiTi TPMS lattice sections fabricated by laser powder bed fusion, Journal of Manufacturing Processes, Volume 102, 2023, Pages 375-386, ISSN 1526-6125, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmapro.2023.07.055.

  2. Hussain, S., Alagha, A.N., & Zaki, W. (2022a). Inhomogeneous Microstructure due to Non-Uniform Solidification Rate in NiTi Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) Structures Fabricated via Laser Powder Bed Fusion." Proceedings of the ASME 2022 International Mechanical Engineering Congress and Exposition. Volume 3: Advanced Materials: Design, Processing, Characterization and Applications; Advances in Aerospace Technology. Columbus, Ohio, USA. October 30–November 3, 2022. V003T03A003. ASME. https://doi.org/10.1115/IMECE2022-95320

  3. Hussain, S., Alagha, A.N., & Zaki, W. (2022b).Imperfections Formation in Thin Layers of NiTi Triply Periodic Minimal Surface Lattices Fabricated Using Laser Powder Bed Fusion. Materials, 15(22), 7950. https://doi.org/10.3390/ma15227950.

entry.title: The Hidden Enemy Inside Every 3D-Printed Metal Lattice — And Why Your Laser Angle Matters More Than You Think

link.title: The Hidden Enemy Inside Every 3D-Printed Metal Lattice — And Why Your Laser Angle Matters More Than You Think

entry.content:
There’s a defect in metal 3D printing that nobody talks about enough. It doesn’t make headlines like delamination failures or visible warping. It forms silently, on the surface of your part, every single time you press print — regardless of how carefully you’ve tuned your laser power or scan speed.

It’s called balling.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

And in a recent study published in Materials (MDPI, 2022), my colleagues and I discovered something that the standard LPBF optimization playbook doesn’t account for: the geometry of your lattice structure and the angle of your laser scan path are independently driving how bad this problem gets — completely separate from the energy density parameters most engineers focus on.

If you’re working with metal additive manufacturing for aerospace, medical devices, or any structural application, this matters more than you might expect.

What is balling, and why should you care?

Imagine you’re laying a bead of solder across a surface. Under the right conditions, it flows out flat and bonds cleanly. Under the wrong conditions — wrong temperature, contaminated surface, wrong speed — it beads up into small spheres instead of spreading. You get little balls instead of a continuous track.

A schematic showing Balling phenomenon in LBPF fabricated samples (courtesy: Gemini)

LPBF does the same thing with metal powder. The laser melts a small pool of powder, and that pool is supposed to wet and fuse to the layer beneath it, building up solid material. When something goes wrong — too much surface tension, oxygen contamination, an unfavorable thermal environment — the melt pool doesn’t spread. Instead, it contracts into spherical balls.

These balls then sit on the surface of your part. They’re poorly bonded. They can obstruct the recoater blade on the next pass. They create stress concentration points. They reduce surface quality. In a porous lattice structure where you’re already working with thin struts and designed void space, they can be especially damaging — blocking pores, altering effective density, and creating initiation sites for cracks.

Most current guidance on avoiding balling focuses on laser process parameters: power, scan speed, and the resulting energy density delivered to the powder bed. Our study found that this picture is incomplete.

What we actually did — and what we found

We printed Schwartz Primitive TPMS lattice layers from NiTi shape memory alloy powder using an EOS M400 metal printer. We kept laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, and layer thickness constant throughout — and varied two things independently:

1. Relative density: samples ranging from 30% to 60% solid volume fraction 2. Scan strategy: four different approaches — parallel with 90° interlayer rotation, parallel with 0° rotation, inclined at 45°, and spiral.

The idea was to isolate the effect of structural design and scan direction from the laser energy variables that dominate most published optimization work.

What we found was clear enough to make you rethink your design workflow.

Finding 1: Denser lattices produce larger balling defects

This one surprised us. You might expect that a denser structure — more solid material, more connected struts — would give the laser more stable material to melt into and produce cleaner results. The opposite was true.

As relative density increased from 30% to 60%, the average size of balling defects grew. At 60% density, balls in the 50–80 µm range were significantly more prevalent than in the 30% density samples, which showed predominantly smaller balls in the 20–50 µm range.

The likely explanation relates to heat balance. In a porous structure, the surrounding void space and the thin struts create a specific thermal environment around each melt pool. As density increases, the local thermal mass changes — more solid material surrounds each melt event, altering how heat flows away from the melt pool and how quickly it solidifies. The result is a melt pool dynamic that favors the formation of larger, more prominent balling imperfections.

There was also a non-monotonic trend in cracking. Samples at 40–50% relative density showed less cracking than those at either extreme (30% or 60%). This suggests there’s a density window — at least for this alloy and these parameters — where the thermal gradients during solidification are more manageable. This kind of non-obvious optimum is exactly why empirical characterization matters, and why assuming a monotonic relationship between density and defect formation can lead you astray.

Finding 2: A 45° scan angle makes balling significantly worse

Of the four scan strategies tested, the inclined 45° strategy produced the most pronounced balling — noticeably worse than the parallel strategies with either 0° or 90° interlayer rotation.

Why? Scan angle affects how heat builds up and dissipates across the powder bed. When the laser traces diagonal paths across a square lattice geometry, the relationship between scan vector length, melt pool geometry, and the local thermal boundary conditions created by the lattice architecture changes in ways that promote balling. The inclined strategy essentially creates a mismatch between the scan path geometry and the structural geometry of the lattice — and the melt pool pays for it.

The parallel strategy with 90° interlayer rotation performed best overall. This is consistent with other literature showing that rotating the scan direction between layers promotes more uniform temperature distribution across the build, reducing residual stress gradients and giving the melt pool a more stable thermal environment to solidify within.

Crucially, average ball sizes across all scan strategies were in the 40–60 µm range — confirming that once balling occurs, the scan strategy influences its severity but not its fundamental presence. You can choose parameters that make it worse; avoiding it entirely requires a different approach.

The underlying physics in plain language

Both findings — density effect and scan angle effect — trace back to the same root cause: the thermal history of the melt pool is controlled not just by your laser settings, but by the local structural environment the laser is operating in.

In a solid block of metal, the thermal environment is relatively uniform and predictable. Each melt pool is surrounded by similar material on all sides, and the heat extraction geometry is consistent throughout the build. Standard parameter optimization works well in this regime.

In a porous TPMS lattice, this assumption breaks down. Each point in the structure has a different relationship to its surrounding geometry — some regions of a thin strut are near void space, others are near junctions with adjacent struts, others are near the build plate. The laser deposits the same energy at each point, but the thermal response is different everywhere. Scan angle then determines which parts of the geometry the laser interacts with first and in what sequence, adding another layer of complexity.

This is why you can optimize your LPBF parameters on dense coupons, transfer those parameters to a lattice design, and still get significant defects — the parameters that worked in the coupon were optimized for a thermal environment that no longer exists in the lattice.

What this means for engineers and designers

Design for printability, not just for performance. When you select a TPMS topology and relative density for an application — whether it’s a bone implant, a heat exchanger insert, or an impact-absorbing structure — that choice is also a choice about printability. Higher densities may give you better mechanical performance on paper but worse as-printed quality. There’s a tradeoff that needs to be quantified, not assumed away.

Don’t default to 45° scan strategies for complex lattice geometries. The 45° inclined strategy is often recommended for residual stress reduction in solid or near-solid parts. Our results suggest this recommendation doesn’t transfer cleanly to porous architected structures — at least not for NiTi TPMS. Test it explicitly rather than inheriting it from dense-part best practices.

Include geometry as a variable in your process qualification. Current process qualification approaches for AM typically involve printing test coupons and characterizing material properties. For lattice structures, this is insufficient. The geometry itself is a process variable. Qualification needs to include the specific topology and density range of the intended application.

Balling is not eliminated by parameter optimization alone. Our results, combined with the broader literature, suggest that balling in LPBF is a persistent feature of the process rather than a defect that can be fully optimized away for complex geometries. The practical goal is managing its severity and understanding its distribution — not assuming it can be eliminated by tweaking energy density alone.

The bigger picture: What’s missing from how we talk about AM quality

There’s a tendency in additive manufacturing — especially in commercial contexts — to describe LPBF as a mature, well-controlled process where the main remaining challenge is material qualification and post-processing. For simple geometries and well-characterized alloys, there’s some truth to that.

For complex architected structures in shape memory alloys, we’re not there yet. Not even close.

The interactions between geometry, process parameters, material behavior, and thermal history in LPBF of NiTi TPMS lattices are still being mapped. Each paper in this space — including this one — adds a piece of that map. The finding that scan strategy and relative density independently drive defect formation in ways that existing process windows don’t predict is exactly the kind of result that needs to be built into design tools, process standards, and quality assurance frameworks.

Until it is, engineers working with these structures need to approach process selection empirically, characterize their as-printed quality rather than assuming it, and resist the temptation to transfer process parameters from one structural context to another without validation.

A closing thought

When I started this work, I expected process parameters to dominate the results. Laser power, energy density, scan speed — these are the levers the AM community has spent the most time studying, and they’re the first things engineers reach for when something goes wrong.

What the data showed was more interesting: the shape of your part and the angle of your laser path are competing with those parameters for control over what actually happens in the melt pool. For a class of structures as geometrically distinctive as TPMS lattices, that competition matters enormously.

It’s a reminder that in materials engineering, the variables you don’t control are often as important as the ones you do.

This article is based on: Hussain, S.; Alagha, A.N.; Zaki, W. “Imperfections Formation in Thin Layers of NiTi Triply Periodic Minimal Surface Lattices Fabricated Using Laser Powder Bed Fusion.” Materials 2022, 15, 7950. https://doi.org/10.3390/ma15227950

entry.title: Why Your 3D-Printed Metal Part Looks Perfect on the Outside — But Isn’t on the Inside

link.title: Why Your 3D-Printed Metal Part Looks Perfect on the Outside — But Isn’t on the Inside

entry.content:
There’s a moment every materials researcher dreads: you’ve spent weeks optimizing your laser parameters, printed a beautiful lattice structure, and when you finally cut it open and look inside under the electron microscope — it’s chaos.

Not catastrophic failure. Not obvious defects. Just... inconsistency. Fine grains here. Coarse grains there. Columnar growth in one region, equiaxed grains in the next. A microstructural fingerprint so complex it almost looks random.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

That moment happened to me while working on one of the more exciting challenges in advanced manufacturing: 3D printing NiTi (Nickel-Titanium) shape memory alloys into triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) lattice structures. And what we found changes how I think about the reliability of metal additive manufacturing — and should change how industry evaluates it too.

First, let me tell you why this material combination matters

NiTi shape memory alloys are remarkable. They’re the material behind self-expanding heart stents, orthodontic wires that apply constant gentle pressure, and experimental morphing aerospace components. When you cool them down and deform them, they snap back to their original shape when heated. When processed correctly, they can also be superelastic — recovering strains far beyond what ordinary steel can handle without any heat needed at all.

TPMS structures — Triply Periodic Minimal Surface lattices — are a class of architected geometries with mathematically smooth, curved surfaces that repeat in three dimensions. Think of them as nature-inspired scaffolding: the Gyroid and Schwarz Primitive topologies you might have seen in biology textbooks or engineering papers. These structures are prized for their exceptional surface-area-to-volume ratios, mechanical efficiency, and permeability — making them candidates for bone implants, heat exchangers, and impact-absorbing crash structures.

Put the two together — NiTi + TPMS — and you theoretically have a smart, porous, biocompatible structure that could change a patient’s implant, absorb impact, or morph on demand. The promise is enormous.

The challenge? Actually printing it.

The problem with printing shapes that have never existed before

Conventional manufacturing routes — machining, casting, forging — struggle badly with NiTi. The alloy’s superelasticity, which makes it so useful in service, makes it a nightmare to machine. It springs back, work-hardens unpredictably, and resists welding. You essentially can’t make a porous NiTi scaffold through traditional means at any reasonable complexity.

Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) changes that equation. It builds parts layer by layer from metal powder using a focused laser beam, enabling geometries that were simply impossible before. For porous, complex structures like TPMS lattices, LPBF isn’t just convenient — it’s the only practical route.

But LPBF introduces its own problem: the laser creates, melts, and resolidifies material millions of times across a build. Each tiny melt pool heats and cools at extreme rates. And when your geometry is complex — when you have curved overhanging surfaces, thin struts, and varying local mass distributions — the thermal history of each point in the part becomes wildly different from every other point.

That’s what we set out to investigate.

What we found when we looked inside

We printed two TPMS geometries — the Schwarz Primitive and the Schoen Gyroid — from pre-alloyed NiTi powder using an EOS M400-4 metal printer at Khalifa University. Same laser parameters for both. Same energy density of 74.1 J/mm³. Same scanning strategy.

When we sectioned the parts and examined them under a scanning electron microscope, the results were striking.

Scanning Electron Microscope Images of LPBF manufactured NiTi Gyroid Lattice showing inhomogeneous microstructural features in a single sample

Both structures showed severe microstructural inhomogeneity. In a single micrograph spanning just 30 micrometres, we could identify up to ten distinct microstructural regions: very fine grains, equiaxed grains, elongated grains, columnar growth, dendritic structures, and transitional zones between them — all within the same printed layer.

This matters because microstructure dictates mechanical properties. A region of fine grains will behave differently under load than a region of large columnar grains. A part that looks geometrically perfect on the outside may have property gradients running through it that no post-print inspection can easily detect.

There was also a geometry effect. The Gyroid, with its more complex curved geometry and nearly double the surface area per unit cell compared to the Primitive, showed significantly more columnar grain growth. The geometry itself — not just the laser settings — was influencing how the melt pool solidified. The shape of the structure was writing its thermal history, and that history was being preserved in the microstructure.

We also observed macro-scale defects driven by the same thermal instability: balling (spherical metal droplets formed by surface tension), porosity, cracking, and uneven surface formation. At the laser parameters tested, warping also limited the build height to just 1–1.5 mm before the printer’s recoater blade was obstructed.

What this means if you’re building products

If you’re an engineer or product developer working with metal additive manufacturing, here’s what I’d draw from this work:

1. Geometry is a process parameter. When you design a complex architected structure for LPBF, you’re not just specifying a shape — you’re specifying a thermal boundary condition that will influence every melt pool in the build. Thin walls, large overhangs, and varying cross-sections all create local thermal environments that can produce dramatically different microstructures. This needs to be designed for, not discovered after the fact.

2. Same process parameters ≠ same material properties. The common assumption that dialling in your laser power, speed, and hatch spacing will give you consistent material is only true for simple, solid geometries. Once you introduce architectural complexity, those parameters interact with geometry in ways that produce inhomogeneous results. Quality assurance strategies need to account for this.

3. Inspection strategies must evolve. Surface finish inspection and even CT scanning have limits when it comes to detecting microstructural gradients. For safety-critical applications — medical implants, aerospace structures, load-bearing components — the field needs better process monitoring and in-situ quality assurance tools. Real-time thermal imaging during the build, as pioneered by other researchers, is one promising direction.

4. The potential remains enormous — but so does the engineering challenge. Nothing in this work diminishes the promise of NiTi TPMS structures. It clarifies the engineering challenge. Inhomogeneous microstructures are not unique to NiTi — they’re a fundamental characteristic of LPBF-built metals. Understanding them is the first step to controlling them.

Where I see this going

The next frontier in this space isn’t just printing these structures — it’s printing them with controlled microstructure. That means:

  • Geometry-aware process planning: slicing software that adjusts laser parameters region by region based on local geometry

  • Real-time feedback control: using thermal sensors and machine learning to detect and correct thermal anomalies during the build

  • Post-process heat treatment optimization: tailored annealing cycles that homogenize microstructure without destroying the designed geometry

  • Computational microstructure prediction: models that predict grain structure from first principles, enabling virtual qualification before a single gram of powder is consumed

This is the intersection of computational design, advanced manufacturing, and materials characterization where the most impactful work will happen over the next decade — and where academic research needs to connect directly with industrial application.

This article is based on research presented at the ASME International Mechanical Engineering Congress and Exposition (IMECE) 2022, Columbus, Ohio. The work was conducted at the Advanced Digital and Additive Manufacturing Center, Khalifa University of Science and Technology, Abu Dhabi, UAE, with support from Khalifa University Grant No. CIRA-2019-024.

entry.title: Digital Twin to Physical Part: Inspecting the Geometry of NiTi Lattices

link.title: Digital Twin to Physical Part: Inspecting the Geometry of NiTi Lattices

entry.content:
In my previous post, I discussed the challenges of 3D printing Nitinol. But before a single laser finishes a scan, the success of the part is determined in the digital realm.

To provide a deeper look into the architecture I’ve been researching, I have uploaded the Gyroid TPMS lattice to Sketchfab. This interactive model allows you to inspect the very geometry that makes these “smart” structures so effective for bone implants and aerospace actuators.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

3D CAD Model of TPMS Gyroid Lattice

Why the Gyroid?

The Gyroid is a “Triply Periodic Minimal Surface” (TPMS). Unlike traditional strut-based lattices, the Gyroid features:

  • Continuous Curvature: This eliminates sharp corners where stress usually concentrates, leading to better fatigue life.

  • High Permeability: The open, interconnected pores are ideal for fluid flow (heat exchangers) and nutrient transport (biomedical scaffolds).

  • High Surface-to-Volume Ratio: This maximizes the functional area for shape memory effects.

Interactive 3D Lab

You can rotate, zoom, and inspect the internal channels of the lattice below. I recommend looking closely at the wall transitions—these are the areas where process parameters like energy density become critical to prevent the “balling” effect I mentioned previously.

Link to Gyroid 3D Model

From Mesh to Metal

Designing these structures requires specialized software (like MSLattice) and a deep understanding of how STL files translate to laser paths. By sharing this model, my goal is to provide a transparent look at the “Digital Twin” of the specimens used in my study, “Microstructural and surface analysis of NiTi TPMS lattice sections fabricated by laser powder bed fusion.”

How do you see architected materials changing your industry? I’d love to hear your thoughts in the comments or via a direct message.

entry.title: 3D Printing the Future of Smart Materials: From Lab to Industry

link.title: 3D Printing the Future of Smart Materials: From Lab to Industry

entry.content:
The Challenge: Why Machining Nitinol is a Nightmare

Nickel-Titanium (NiTi) shape memory alloys are prized for their unique ability to “remember” shapes, high damping capacity, and biocompatibility. However, their high ductility and superior strength make them incredibly difficult to machine using traditional subtractive methods. Tooling wears out quickly, and complex geometries are often impossible to achieve—until now.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The Solution: LPBF & Architected Porosity

CAD models of architected lattices (a) Gyroid TPMS Lattice, (b) Primitive TPMS Lattice, (c) Gyroid Lattice Unit Cell, and (d) Primitive Lattice Unit Cell

Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) allows us to bypass traditional machining by building parts layer-by-layer. My recent research focused on a specific family of architected materials called Triply Periodic Minimal Surfaces (TPMS), including “Gyroid” and “Primitive” topologies. These structures aren’t just visually striking; they offer a massive surface-to-volume ratio and high strength-to-weight performance that is critical for industrial applications.

Key Industrial Takeaways

  • Sector Applications: These architected NiTi structures have transformative potential in Biomedical implants (matching bone stiffness to prevent stress shielding), Aerospace and Automotive (light-weighting and energy absorption), and Robotics (high-density actuators).

  • The “Energy Density” Threshold: For industry, process stability is everything. Our study found that surface quality is highly dependent on volumetric energy density. Specifically:

    • Primitive structures achieve even surfaces at a threshold of 48 J/mm³.

    • Gyroid structures require a ~12.5% higher threshold of 54 J/mm³ to prevent surface defects and pores.

  • Managing Material Loss: A critical industrial challenge identified was Nickel evaporation and the formation of oxide-rich phases. Since the Ni/Ti ratio dictates the material’s “memory” temperature, controlling laser power and scanning speed is vital to ensure the final part performs as intended.

  • Overcoming the Balling Phenomenon: A major hurdle in scaling LPBF is the “balling” issue—where the molten track breaks into spheres rather than forming a continuous weld. Our analysis shows that this occurs primarily at higher scanning speeds due to Plateau-Rayleigh instability. In industrial production, this creates high surface roughness and internal voids that can lead to premature structural failure. By fine-tuning the balance between laser power and speed, we can suppress balling to ensure the structural integrity of thin-walled TPMS lattices.

  • Design for Manufacturing (DfM): We observed that structural geometry directly influences the cooling rate. Gyroid lattices, with their higher surface areas, dissipate heat faster, which can lead to finer grain structures compared to primitive designs.

Balling issue in LPBF of Nitinol Primitive TPMS Lattice

The Bottom Line for Industry

Additive manufacturing of TPMS lattices turns NiTi from a “hard-to-work” material into a programmable engineering tool. By optimizing laser parameters to the specific geometry of the part, we can now produce components with tailored porosity and functional performance that were previously unachievable.

Further Reading & Technical Data

This article is based on my peer-reviewed research published in the Journal of Manufacturing Processes. For a deeper dive into the microstructural evolution and surface roughness analysis of these structures, you can access the full paper here:

Source: Hussain, S., Alagha, A. N., Haidemenopoulos, G. N., & Zaki, W. (2023). Microstructural and surface analysis of NiTi TPMS lattice sections fabricated by laser powder bed fusion. Journal of Manufacturing Processes, 102, 375-386. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.manpro.2023.07.010]

entry.title: The Researcher in 3D Printing and Metamaterials

link.title: The Researcher in 3D Printing and Metamaterials

entry.content:
The Mission

I am Dr. Shahadat Hussain, an engineer and researcher dedicated to the intersection of materials science, advanced manufacturing, and computational design.

My work is driven by a central question: How can we design internal structures to give materials extraordinary properties? From 3D-printed shape memory alloys to complex TPMS (Triply Periodic Minimal Surface) lattices, I explore the frontier of what is physically possible through additive manufacturing.

Thanks for reading Shahadat's Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

My Background

Currently, I serve as a Research Associate at New York University in Abu Dhabi. My journey in science and engineering has taken me from a PhD in Materials Science and Technology (AcSIR, India) to deep-diving into the mechanics of “smart” materials. I worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Khalifa University prior to the current affiliation.

Over the years, I’ve developed a specialized toolkit that includes:

  • Additive Manufacturing: Mastering Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) and FFF.

  • Smart Materials: Exploring the “memory” of NiTi and Cu-based alloys.

  • Computational Design: Using Python, SQL, and Data Science to predict how materials will behave before they are even printed.

Why I Started This Substack

The world of materials science can often feel locked behind paywalls and dense academic jargon. I created this space to pull back the curtain on:

  1. Technical Deep-Dives: Breaking down the latest trends in metamaterials and 3D printing.

  2. Research Insights: Sharing the “ah-ha” moments (and the failures) from my lab work at Khalifa University.

  3. The Digital Lab: Discussing how Data Science and Scientific Computing are changing the way we do engineering.

Stay Connected

Whether you are a fellow researcher, a student, or someone fascinated by the future of manufacturing, I’m glad you’re here. By subscribing, you’ll get my latest insights and research updates delivered directly to your inbox.

Let’s build something extraordinary.
